image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   - A **flow / alluvial-style line chart** showing how U.S. states move across partisan margin positions over multiple election years.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Single-panel layout** (not faceted).
   - Uses **flowing lines** to connect the same state across years.
   - States are arranged by **horizontal position within each election year**.
   - **Color** separates Democratic-leaning vs Republican-leaning positions, with a neutral center for ties.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Election year | Temporal | Position on y-axis (rows: 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020) |
| State | Categorical/nominal | Individual flow line identity; text labels at selected positions |
| Partisan margin / partisan lean | Quantitative | Position on x-axis relative to center (“Tie”), with labeled reference points such as +10, +20, +30, +40 Dem./Rep. |
| Party direction (Democratic vs Republican side) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (blue for Democratic side, red for Republican side) |
| Winning candidate by year | Categorical/nominal | Text labels next to each year on the left (e.g., George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Donald J. Trump, Joseph R. Biden Jr.) |

comments.raw_comment:
Headline: The States Are Covering the Spread...Sadly
1. I’m particularly noticing how spread out all of these states are right now compared to what they were in 2004. This indicates that states are starting to shift farther from a balance between republican and democrats, becoming strongholds by the year. The spread of states from a tie indicates how polarized our country is becoming, since each state is becoming strongly associated with one party or another. Therefore, our elections are constantly being decided by the few swing states. Only these states have a major influence due to the landslides every year in other states. I hope the parties won’t give up on trying to flip a state even if it seems out of reach. I also hope voters believe their vote makes a difference. Then all 50 states will contribute to electing future presidents. 
2. 
I wonder if parties will still spend time trying to win the voters of the states they had but now have lost. I think they should absolutely do so. Georgia was out of reach for Democrats in 2004 but has flipped blue in this most recent election. With this strategy both parties can win back states they previously had. 
3. 
Being from Boston, this will likely have a miniscule effect on my state. Massachusetts hasn’t flipped red since Regan and they have been shifting more left ever since. What I will say is that in General Presidential Elections, candidates will likely not campaign in Mass., for it is almost guaranteed Mass. will go blue.

comments.raw_comment:
I noticed that the graph shows the difference in party shifts in the United States for the past 5 presidential elections using red snd blue lines. I noticed that both lines bent towards the democratic party in 2004-2008, depicting that people don’t always vote “red or blue” every year, but select different candidates depending on their ideologic preferences, not just a default side. The following years illustrate the same concept, that democrats don’t always vote blue and republicans don’t always vote red, but both parties for the candidate with political philosophy and plans most aligning to their own, often independent of “red” or “blue.”
I wonder why in 2012,  some states voted almost completely republicans and others almost completely democratic.  I wonder if the further division caused by the media was a factor in why the 2020 election had some states exceptionally blue and others exceptionally red. I also wonder why states like Utah, Hawaii, and North Carolina had such a fluid change in the voting in these elections.
An impact that this could have is thats it is less likely for more worthy candidates to run for president given the amount of backlash they receive, republican or democrat. It’s also less likely that there will be as many voters next election because this year, neither candidate was liked very much; most people said they had to choose the “lesser of two evils.” 
Catchy Headline:  Swinging Left and Right

Title: Intricacies of American Politics Made Visual 

Context makes the graph all the more intriguing. Obama (in 2008) was able to increase the margin of victory in HI by a startling 35 points; so too was Mitt Romney (in 2012) able to increase the margin of victory in UT by a likewise startling 20 points. Obama is a HI native; Romney, the first Mormon to head a major party presidential ticket, hails from UT, the only Mormon-majority state. The prospect of "one of your own" in the White House caused Hawaiians and Utahans to turn out in record numbers. This begs the question: in the "United States" of America, why might your identity as a citizen of a state trump your identity as an American? Does love of state top love of country? In an age where voter turnout teeters around a measly 50%, Republicans and Democrats alike need to analyze the intricacy of factors that drive voter turnout up or down. Americans like to boast a rational electorate, but this may not be so. In an increasingly contentious political atmosphere, it's important to analyze how a voter's personal identity and sense of reason intersect to manifest as a vote for either candidate. The concept of identity is central to every human being and everything that human does; politics is no exception to this, for better or worse.

I noticed that the votes are unpredictable. In 2004, the number of votes for each party's candidate was almost with there being slightly more Republican voters. In 2008, quite a few states turned blue and voted for Obama. When it came to his reelection in 2012, he had fewer votes as a couple of states turned back to red but still had enough votes to win. However, in 2016, these same swing states turned red. For the 2020 election, some states flipped again and voted blue, while some states remained red. For each party, however, there are states that haven't flipped for any election. 

I wonder what this graph would look like for past elections and what it will look like in the future. I also wonder what characterizes a swing state and what causes it to flip almost every election. I notice that over the course of the 16 years, voting by party has varied for many states. In 2004, the two sides are almost symmetrical, but if anything, more states had more republican voters. Then in 2008, there was a significant swing to the left, as many states who had a moderate number of Republican voters in 2004, voted for Barack Obama in 2008. Between 2012 and 2020, the two sides mostly evened out again, with some states varying back and forth. In 2020 it appears the lines are starting to pull left again, which makes sense considering Biden won the election and several swing states has voted in his favor. Although the lines are quite curved, which shows they shifted a lot, however, throughout, there are states that stayed strongly to one of either side, showing that recently the country has been extremely divided by political parties. I wonder why Barack Obama so strongly pulled so many voters from swing states and even weak/moderate republican voting states? And why did they swing back to republican voting the next year? This impacts me and my community because it shows how divided our country is and this division has recently been creating a lot of struggles in our country. It's scary because the media in predominantly republican areas displays very different coverage than I get living in Massachusetts, therefore, I feel political parties continue to get even more divided until this problem is solved.

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that most of the states that flipped between the years 2004-2020 were more moderate in the 2004 election than the states that did not flip. Between the 2004 and 2008 election, almost every state's votes (even Republican ones) became more Democratic. Between the 2008 and 2012 election, most state's votes became more Republican. In the last two elections (2016 and 2020) the state's votes changed by a smaller degree and more randomly. In the last two elections, there was neither a more Democratic trend nor a more Republican trend between all the states. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder why so many more people voted Democratic in the 2008 election, and I wonder why so many more people voted Republican in the 2012 election. Is it because people were unsatisfied with the Presidents of the time? Were they hoping for a more radical change by flipping their votes?

What impact does this have on you and your community?
I live in a state that has voted Democratic since 2004. Since 2004, my state's slightly more Democratic, a fact that I am not surprised by. Thus, party shifting does not impact my community as much as it might impact people in Vermont or Ohio. However, as party views become more one-sided in my state, my community's values tend to surround me in school and on social media.

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that in the 2008 election of President Barack Obama states that were already blue went more democratic, a couple of swing states that voted red in the 2004 election went blue, and states that voted very republican in the 2004 election shifted more to the left, towards the democrats.

In the 2016 and 2020 election, no states voted very democratic (+40 Dem.). A majority of the states in the 2016 election voted more towards the right and swing states voted republican. I wonder why in each election, except 2012, the president keeps shifting from one party to another party. Maybe it's because people aren't satisfied with the state of the country and think the other party, that's not currently in office, can make life better for Americans.

This effects my community because I live in NJ, a primarily blue state. Although NJ hasn't voted Republican since 1988, I notice a lot of my classmates and a growing amount of people in my community are conservative. It will be interesting to see when/if New Jersey will vote Republican again and what factors will push them towards voting red.

A headline I would give this article is “Close Call For America, But the Country is Becoming Bluer”.
